Karl,

I've done a few tests and it looks to me like parallel is able to split the work across multiple cores on a single compute node, but is not effectively splitting the work across multiple compute nodes. For example, an analysis using 8 cores on one compute node (n.cluster=8) and and an analysis using 8 cores on each of two compute nodes (n.cluster=16) both in practice only use 8 cores and both take an equivalent amount of time.

I think RAM isn't a limiting factor. I've been allocating 3Gb of RAM per core/cluster, and they seem to use about 1.7Gb of that. I've done the same analysis doubling the RAM with no increase in speed.

Is there a possible solution for getting the parallel package to perform in a high performance computing cluster?

Thanks again,

Chris

Yes, within an instance of R, scantwo permutations won't be split across nodes but will just use the multiple CPUs within a node. I don't know how to split a task across multiple nodes from within R, and from what I'd seen in the distant past, it would be quite system-dependent.

Personally, I'd just creat a bunch of R scripts for separate R CMD BATCH runs, and then use your job scheduler to spawn and manage the jobs.

karl

messages.subject: Re: changing names/order of linkage groups
messages.body_plain:
> R/qtl infers linkage groups and numbers them in decreasing order of size (number of markers). In your tutorial, the inferred 5 linkage groups are also in decreasing order of length, i.e. size is proportional to the length.
>
> I have now inferred 7 linkage groups, which have been numbered in decreasing order of size (no. of markers). However, the size is not proportional to the length. As an example, an LG with 48 markers is shorter that that with 28 markers.
>
> Could you please tell me what to do?

You can name the linkage groups whatever you want.

If you want to change the names, do something like the following. This code changes the names of linkage groups 4 and 5:

  names(mycross$geno) <- c("1", "2", "3", "5", "4", "6", "7")

You can change the order that they appear in the cross this way:

  mycross$geno <- mycross$geno[c(1, 2, 3, 5, 4, 6, 7)]

karl

messages.subject_clean: Mapping in a BC2, BC3 mixed population.
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am analyzing data from a large plant population of 476 inbred lines.  The population was made by our colleagues and comprises a mix of BC2 and BC3 lines that were inbred for 4 generations before we sequenced and phenotyped them.

We know which lines are BC2 and which BC3.  I know such a mixed crossing scheme presents complications for QTL mapping, but nevertheless was hoping to analyze our data with R/qtl.

As a first stab I am thinking of analyzing the data twice, once specifying the crossing scheme as BC2 and another as BC3.  However, since we know which lines are BC2 and BC3, would it be possible to analyze the data as a BC2/BC3 combination?

I realize the answer is probably no, at least not without extending the capabilities of R/qtl.  Nonetheless, I wonder if it's at all feasible to do so, and how hard such an extension of the codebase might be.

Any other suggestions or advice regarding mapping with this mixed scheme would be greatly appreciated!!

Thanks in advance for your help!!
Dan Fulop.

Hi,

I’m attempting to map a  behavioural phenotype in a backcross that takes the form of counts of successes and failures (actually courtships by an individual towards one species of butterfly or another). One way to do this, I guess, is to convert the data to a proportion and arcsin transform it before using scan one in R/qtl etc.

model <- glm (cbind(num_successes, num_failures) ~ trait, family = binomial)

I believe this in affect does a weighted regression.

null_model <- glm (cbind(num_successes, num_failures) ~ 1, family = binomial)

My first question is whether: logLik (model) - logLik(null_model) would give me an appropriate LOD score (I’ve then run a permutation test to check for significance of peaks).

Second, is there a way to do this with interval mapping to account for missing data and gaps between genotypes. Is ‘weights’ (as scanone argument) relevant - assuming I transform the proportions data -  I can’t find much on this.

I thought it might be possible to use the code I’ve written  iterated over genotypes imputated using sim.geno (but I can’t work out how to get these simulated genotypes out) to produce LOD score across the markers and gaps?

That’s a lot of questions. Thanks for any help.

cheers,

Richard Merrill

messages.body_plain:
If you have reasonably dense markers and no selective genotyping, then the simplest solution would be Haley-Knott regression.  That is you regress on the genotype probabilities between marker locations.  Run "calc.genoprob" to calculate genotype probabilities, use "pull.genoprob" to get them out as a matrix, and then use "glm" as in the code snippet you showed.

data(listeria)
listeria <- calc.genoprob(listeria, step=1, stepwidth="max")
pr <- pull.genoprob(listeria, chr=c(5,13), omit.first.prob=TRUE, include.pos.info <http://include.pos.info>=TRUE)

You can pull out imputations in the same way using "sim.geno" instead of "calc.genoprob" and "pull.draws" instead of "pull.genoprob".  There is a tricky step afterward of averaging the log-likelihoods from the different imputations.  A trimmed mean is taken, instead of a straight average. This step is explained in the Sen and Churchill (2001) paper.  I can elaborate if you wish.

With regards,
Saunak

messages.subject_clean: Rqtl: How do I find out what alleles A and B were coded as?
messages.body_plain:
> I'm working with doubled haploid wheat lines and am using R/qtl to map rust resistance genes. I read available pdfs but there is one thing I cannot find. There are examples in your pdfs where allele A is coded 0.5 and allele B -0.5,
> how can I 1. tell R how I want them coded,

Currently, you can't modify the coding scheme.

> 2. if done automatically how do I get get the info from R what was coded? I cannot find an output where I clearly see what allele A and B where coded as and need to be 100% sure that I'm interpreting the results from the allele effects correctly.

The coding is described in the help file for fitqtl:

"The estimated QTL effects for a backcross are derived by the coding scheme +/- 1/2 for AA and AB, so that the additive effect corresponds to the difference between phenotype averages for the two genotypes. For doubled haploids and RIL, the coding scheme is +/- 1 for AA and BB, so that the additive effect corresponds to half the difference between the phenotype averages for the two homozygotes.

"For an intercross, the additive effect is derived from the coding scheme -1/0/+1 for genotypes AA/AB/BB, and so is half the difference between the phenotype averages for the two homozygotes. The dominance deviation is derived from the coding scheme 0/+1/0 for genotypes AA/AB/BB, and so is the difference between the phenotype average for the heterozygotes and the midpoint between the phenotype averages for the two homozygotes."

I'd recommend checking such things "by hand".

For example, you could use fitqtl with a single-QTL model and compare the effect to what you get when you just calculate the difference in phenotype averages.

Here's some example code:

  data(fake.bc)
  fake.bc <- calc.genoprob(fake.bc)
  out <- scanone(fake.bc)
  max(out) # maximum LOD at D5M394 (chr 5 at 9.8 cM)

  # difference in means
  g <- pull.geno(fill.geno(fake.bc))[,"D5M394"]
  y <- pull.pheno(fake.bc, 1)
  me <- tapply(y, g, mean, na.rm=TRUE)
  diff(me) # 0.95

  # fitqtl
  qtl <- makeqtl(fake.bc, chr=5, pos=9.8, what="prob")
  outfq <- fitqtl(fake.bc, qtl=qtl, get.ests=TRUE, method="hk")
  summary(outfq) # estimated effect: 0.975

  # fitqtl, pretending these are doubled haploids
  class(fake.bc)[1] <- "dh"
  outfq <- fitqtl(fake.bc, qtl=qtl, get.ests=TRUE, method="hk")
  summary(outfq) # estimated effect: 0.488

karl
